question: A recent case in Greece concerning the alleged sexual exploitation of minors through online advertisements highlights the growing risks linked to the digital dimension of trafficking in human beings. Directive 2011/36/EU, as amended by Directive (EU) 2024/1712, covers trafficking in human beings for the purpose of sexual exploitation and further protects children.

In particular, the directive recognises the role of the internet and social media in recruiting, advertising and exploiting victims and underlines the need to strengthen the digital capabilities of the competent authorities, prevention and the early identification of victims.

In parallel, Article 28 of Regulation (EU) 2022/2065 on digital services (DSA) obliges platforms accessible to minors to take appropriate and proportionate measures to ensure that they enjoy a high level of privacy, safety and security. Can the Commission answer the following: 1.

Is there any information on the transposition of Directive (EU) 2024/1712 into Greek law, in particular as regards the prevention and detection of cases of online recruitment and sexual exploitation of minors, as well as the early recognition of the related risks?
What specific measures is the Commission taking under the DSA, and in particular under Article 28 thereof, to effectively limit related risks on online platforms?

Does the Commission intend to strengthen cooperation between Digital Services Coordinators, law enforcement and judicial authorities and national anti-trafficking bodies in order to speed up the detection and investigation of suspicious online advertisements linked to the trafficking and sexual exploitation of minors?
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (26.11.2026) Member States had to transpose Directive (EU) 2024/17121 on preventing and combating trafficking in human beings and protecting its victims by 15 July 2026.

On 25 September 2026, the Commission opened an infringement procedure by sending a letter of formal notice to Greece, along with 19 other Member States that had not communicated their national transposition measures by the deadline. Greece has two months to respond and to notify its complete transposition measures.

Regarding Article of the 28 Digital Services Act2, the Commission has adopted and published guidelines under Article 28(4)3 to help online platforms ensure a high level of privacy, safety and security for minors, including in cases of platform-facilitated child trafficking. The Commission has taken steps to strengthen cooperation between Digital Services Coordinators, law enforcement and judicial authorities.
Human trafficking was discussed at the 13th and 14th meetings of Working Group 7 of the European Board for Digital Services4.

The Commission will continue cooperating with Digital Service Coordinators, law enforcement, judicial authorities and national anti-trafficking coordinators, including under the new EU Strategy on combatting trafficking in human beings5, which places particular emphasis on strengthening engagement with the private sector, including digital industries and online platforms, is a key priority.

Moreover, the framework offered by the European Multidisciplinary Platform Against Criminal Threats will continue to support innovative approaches and digital investigations, including dedicated hackathons aimed at detecting online trafficking activities, identifying potential victims and uncovering criminal networks.
1 Directive (EU) 2024/1712 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 13 June 2024 amending Directive

2011/36/EU on preventing and combating trafficking in human beings and protecting its victims, OJ L, 2024/1712, 24.6.2024. 2 Regulation (EU) 2022/2065 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 19 October 2022 on a Single Market for Digital Services and amending Directive 2000/31/EC (Digital Services Act), OJ L 277, 27.10.2022, pp. 1–102. 3 https://digital-strategy.ec.europa.
